key: Studios can license one title at several return rates
The casino chooses which build it runs
The in-game paytable is the only reliable source
body: A slot is not one machine. Most volume studios ship a title in two or three configurations — typically a headline rate and one or two reduced builds — and the operator picks which it licenses. Nothing in the lobby tells you which one you loaded.

The paytable inside the game does. It states the return for the build you are playing, and it is the figure RTP Watch records, per casino, as our field-testing reaches each operator. Where a reading shows a reduced build we name it in that operator's review rather than the studio's.
Two points of return is not a rounding difference. On $10,000 of turnover it is $200 of expected value moved from you to the house, for exactly the same game and the same session length.

key: Multiply the credit, not the deposit
Game weighting can double the real figure
A max-cashout cap can make the whole offer worthless
body: Wagering is stated as a multiple of the credited amount. At 40× a $100 bonus needs $4,000 of turnover before withdrawal; at 1× it needs $100. That single number moves an offer from useful to unusable, and it is the first thing to find in the terms.

Then read the weighting. If slots count 100% but live tables count 10%, the same requirement takes ten times the volume at a blackjack table. Bonuses that exclude sportsbook entirely are common and rarely stated in the headline.

Finally check the cap. A max cashout of 5× the bonus means a $100 credit can never return more than $500 no matter what you hit, which quietly deletes the tail of the distribution you were playing for.

key: Tiered verification is the norm, not the exception
Cumulative volume is usually the trigger
Verify before you need to, not after a win
body: Most crypto casinos run tiered verification: you can deposit, play and withdraw small amounts unverified, and a document request appears once cumulative volume crosses a threshold. The threshold is rarely published, and an operator can move it without notice.
Withdrawal is the worst moment to discover it. A cash-out routed to verification is one of the most common reasons a payout takes a day instead of minutes.
If you intend to play at any size, verify on a quiet day. It takes a few minutes and removes a common source of withdrawal delay.

key: Seconds to credit, no on-chain fee
Channel capacity caps the amount
Few operators support it, so check the cashier
body: Lightning settles in seconds and avoids on-chain fees entirely, which makes it the correct rail for small, frequent deposits. Where an operator supports it, it is usually the quickest way to a playable balance in bitcoin.
The constraint is capacity. Larger payments are more likely to hit channel limits, and when they do the payment fails rather than arriving slowly, which is confusing the first time it happens.
Support is thin. Each casino profile lists the coins and networks the operator itself names, so check there, and in the cashier, before relying on Lightning.

key: Policies differ by casino, so read the profile
It matters most on small, frequent cash-outs
Chain choice moves it by two orders of magnitude
body: A withdrawal fee deducted from your balance is a real cost, and it compounds if you cash out often. Some operators say they cover the network fee; others pass it through, and some charge a fixed per-coin fee on top. Each casino profile quotes the operator's own wording on withdrawal fees.

The chain matters more than the policy. An Ethereum withdrawal can cost dollars in gas at busy times; the same transfer on Solana costs a fraction of a cent. A fee-absorbing operator on an expensive chain can still be the worse deal.
The coins page explains how each network sets its fee. Check the operator's own withdrawal fee in its cashier before you pick a chain.

key: Hot wallet for play, cold wallet for holdings
Never fund a casino from an exchange address
Assume any on-site balance can be frozen
body: Keep the amount you are willing to lose in a hot wallet, and everything else somewhere that requires a deliberate act to reach. Operators freeze accounts for routine verification more often than players expect, and a frozen balance is out of reach until it clears.
Do not send from an exchange to a cashier directly. Casino addresses are clustered by analytics firms, and the return path is what triggers compliance questions on your exchange account later.
Treat any balance on-site as in transit. The account is a place to play, not a place to keep money.

key: Six areas, every fact cited
Commission is not an input
Gaps are marked, not guessed
body: Every review covers the same six areas: payout speed, bonus fairness, crypto support, trust and licensing, game and RTP quality, and support. There is no score or weighting. A review states what the operator publishes on each, with a citation, so you can check it yourself.
Commercial relationships are not an input. We earn commission when a reader signs up through our links, and the rate is not visible to whoever writes the review. It never changes what a review says.
Where an operator doesn't publish something, the profile says "Not stated" instead of filling the gap with a guess.

key: Margin is the overround baked into the price
Compare across many markets, not one
One point of margin beats any welcome offer
body: Margin, or overround, is the amount by which a book's implied probabilities exceed 100%. It is the sportsbook equivalent of RTP, and unlike a bonus it applies to every bet you place.

To compare books fairly, take the same markets across football, basketball, tennis and esports, at the same time of day, and look at the median rather than one price. Books quote tighter on marquee events and wider on everything else, so a single-market comparison is misleading.
A book a point tighter costs you less over a season than any promotion returns. It is the least visible and most important number on a sportsbook.

key: KYC is the document check that stands between you and your money
Only one of {casinos} operators says it will never run one
The tier an operator sits in is set by its own terms, not its marketing
body: KYC — know your customer — is the point where a casino stops treating you as an anonymous balance and asks who you are. Usually a government ID, often a selfie, sometimes a utility bill. It exists because the licence requires it: an operator that cannot show it checked is an operator that can lose the licence.

For a crypto casino the interesting question is not whether KYC exists. It is when it fires. You can deposit, play and win without ever being asked, and then be asked at the moment you try to take the money out — which is the worst time to discover your name does not match your ID.

We read the stated policy at all {casinos} casinos we track and sorted them by what the policy actually does. {required} make verification a step you complete before you can play or withdraw. {threshold} publish a trigger — a cumulative deposit figure, a withdrawal size, a deadline after your first deposit — so you can see it coming. {discretionary} run no routine check but reserve the right to ask, usually at withdrawal or on anything that looks unusual. {conflicting} contradict themselves across their own pages. And {never} says it will never ask at all.

The tier is not the same as the marketing. Razed calls itself a No-KYC crypto casino; its own AML policy requests ID documents when you withdraw. Bluff usually asks for nothing — unless you opt into a bonus, which makes verification a condition. Degencity lets you deposit, play and withdraw without documents but still wants a verified email address before it pays. Read the second sentence of any no-KYC claim; that is where the conditions live.

What this means in practice: decide before you deposit, not after. If you will not hand over a passport, an operator in the required tier is not for you whatever its bonus looks like — you will hit the wall at cash-out. If you are fine with verification, do it early and on a quiet day rather than at the moment you are trying to withdraw a win. And if an operator's pages disagree with each other, assume the stricter one applies, because that is the one its compliance team works from.

key: Check whether you are eligible before you deposit, not after
Verify on a quiet day — the worst time to start is mid-withdrawal
{threshold} operators publish the exact figure that triggers a check
body: Verification is the step where a casino stops treating you as a balance and asks who you are. It is also where money gets stuck, almost always for the same reason: the account was opened in a hurry, the details did not match the documents, and nobody found out until a withdrawal was already in flight.

**Start with eligibility, before you deposit anything.** Two separate things have to be true. Your country has to allow you to play — that is the law where you are, and it is not the operator's decision. And the operator has to accept your country, which is in its own terms. They disagree more often than you would think: nine countries we cover ban online casinos while most operators' terms do not mention them at all. Our legal map has the first answer and each casino page has the second. Getting this wrong is the one mistake that cannot be fixed later, because a balance built in a place you were never allowed to play is a balance you will not be paid.

**Register with the details that are on your documents.** Legal name as spelled on the ID, date of birth, address as it appears on a recent bill or statement. Not a nickname, not an old address, not a middle name you usually drop. Every mismatch is a manual review, and manual reviews happen at the slowest possible moment. One account per person, in your own name — paying a balance to someone whose name is not on the account is the thing compliance teams are built to stop.

**Then verify, and do it early.** Of the {casinos} casinos we track, {required} make verification a step you complete before you can play or withdraw, and {threshold} publish the figure that triggers it — Cloudbet at $2,200 of cumulative deposits, FortuneJack at $10,000, Winna within 30 days of your first deposit or €2,000 wagered, mBit above 1 BTC. Another {discretionary} run no routine check and reserve the right to ask anyway, usually at the moment you withdraw. Only one says it never will. So the question is not whether you can avoid it; it is whether you do it on a quiet Tuesday or during a cash-out.

**What to have ready.** A government photo ID, usually both sides. A selfie, sometimes holding the document — seven operators ask for one and one wants it from five angles. Proof of address dated within the last three months, which thirteen ask for: a utility bill or bank statement, not a screenshot of an app. Where larger sums are involved you may be asked for source of funds, which means showing where the money came from rather than just who you are. Photograph documents flat, in daylight, with all four corners in frame and nothing cropped — most rejections are a corner out of shot, not a problem with the document.

**Submit through the account itself, never anywhere else.** Open verification from inside your own logged-in session. No legitimate operator asks for identity documents over live chat, email, Telegram, Discord or a link someone sends you, and anyone who does is not the casino. Some route the check through a third-party provider — Duel uses Checkin.com, Solcasino uses Sumsub — which is normal, but you should still arrive there from inside your account rather than from a link.

**If it stalls.** Most delays are a document that was readable to you and not to a reviewer: a glare, a cropped edge, an address that no longer matches. Resubmit a cleaner copy before assuming anything is wrong. If a check is taking longer than the operator's own stated time, ask support through the account and keep the thread. And read the bonus terms before you opt in rather than after — Bluff needs no verification to withdraw unless you took a bonus, at which point it does.
